correctness.rationale: Exact sampling indicators give E f^2=c sum a_i^2 and E f^4=A(sum a_i^2)^2+B sum a_i^4 for all n>=4 and 2<=k<=n-2. Lagrange multipliers on the compact zero-sum unit sphere produce at most three distinct roots. Tangent Hessian signs rule out three-valued minima and all globally maximizing three-valued vectors; all surviving maxima/minima are two-valued. Their kurtoses n/[h(n-h)]-3/n are sharply minimized at balanced multiplicities and maximized at h=1, proving the complete equality classes and sign transition. Independent exact rational subset enumeration of 638 finite profiles confirmed identities and branch values; this computation is not relied upon as a proof in all dimensions.

originality.rationale: The literature establishes Johnson harmonic bases and nonsharp hypercontractive bounds, and studies tail probabilities for the same finite-population sample sum. Their inspected statements do not imply the exact finite (n,k)-dependent L2-to-L4 norm together with complete spike/balanced/resonant equality cases. The fourth moment polynomial itself is an elementary sampling identity and not claimed independently novel. Prior equivalence risk remains for an unindexed sharp sample-kurtosis theorem.
residual_risks: An unindexed or inaccessible sharp finite-population sample-kurtosis theorem might already optimize the same fourth-moment ratio; the 1974 sampling-moments article was available only by abstract.
Primary published harmonic references are partly about adjacent, not identical, functional norms; full historical novelty cannot be certified.

value.rationale: A sharp norm over the full (n-1)-dimensional Johnson first harmonic is a natural exact hypercontractive embedding invariant. Its optimizers genuinely switch from one exceptional coordinate to balanced two-level vectors at the integer surface 6k(n-k)=n(n+1), and at equality every coefficient direction has the same distortion. These are structural, all-dimensional sharpness/equality results rather than one finite experiment or a renaming of the classical moment polynomial. They distinguish sparse sample amplifications from near-Gaussian balanced directions and give exact benchmarks for finite-slice harmonic inequalities.
